That said, conditions in the bay appear active. A Santa Rosa Beach guide reporting about six days ago (approximately July 30) noted a strong speckled trout bite with good numbers and quality fish, plus a notable bull redfish catch — a 40¼-inch, 26-lb fish landed in the bay. Water temp is 85°F at this location. FishingBooker's July Choctawhatchee Bay overview similarly highlights bull redfish and trophy-class trout as the headline inshore targets, with guides recommending early-morning departures to beat summer heat and crowds. The Half Hitch Destin report from July 20 (the most recent retrievable post) focused largely on offshore action, but bay trout had been described as consistent and scattered throughout the system in the weeks prior, with anglers finding fish by being selective about wind-sheltered areas.

aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is fishing well heading into mid-summer, with a Santa Rosa Beach guide reporting a strong speckled trout bite and a notable 40¼-inch, 26-lb bull redfish landed in the bay around July 30 — conditions that should carry into today. Plan around an early start: water temps are sitting at 85°F, storms are possible before 4 PM with a 29% chance, and the best bite window will be the morning hours before heat and weather build. Light WSW winds (0–10 mph) and a Last Quarter moon offer manageable tidal movement, though slightly stained water will favor louder or more visible presentations across the bay.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides and concentrates speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around the pilings year-round. Lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on incoming tides, as fish stack up to intercept passing bait. It's worth noting this is open, exposed water — one of the first spots to become unfishable when wind picks up or weather builds.
bridge.todaysCall: The low tide bottoms out around 10:15 AM, so target the pilings during the incoming push that follows — fish will move to the lee-side pilings as current strengthens through midday. Light WSW winds of 0–10 mph should keep chop manageable in the morning, but keep a close eye on the sky; with storms possible before 4 PM, plan to wrap up at the bridge by early afternoon at the latest. Slightly stained water today means louder or chartreuse-tinted soft plastics and tipped jigs will help fish locate your presentation. The recent strong trout bite reported bay-wide makes the bridge pilings a legitimate shot at quality fish, but have an exit plan given the exposed nature of this spot.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder at the creek mouth where oyster bars are the prime structure. Tree cover keeps the interior a few degrees cooler than the open bay and provides genuine shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish conditions and can hold largemouth bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua is a smart call today — the tree canopy and protected layout offer a buffer against both the 85°F heat and the storm threat before 4 PM, letting you fish longer with less risk than open-water spots. Work the oyster bars at the creek mouth on the incoming tide that builds after the 10:15 AM low; redfish and trout should stack there as current picks up. Slightly stained water calls for darker or chartreuse soft plastics, weedless gold spoons, or noisy topwaters early before the sun gets high. The bay-wide redfish bite has been strong, and Alaqua's sheltered structure makes it one of the better bets to find quality fish without fighting weather exposure.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, which typically means less-educated fish willing to bite. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing water for redfish in under two feet, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It's less protected than LaGrange when weather builds, so factor that in when conditions deteriorate.
basin.todaysCall: The morning window before the storm threat materializes is ideal for sight-fishing Basin Bayou's shallow grass flats — get there early, as 85°F water will push reds into shadows or deeper water as the sun climbs. Low tide at 10:15 AM will concentrate fish on defined edges and creek mouths, and the incoming tide that follows is your best window for working the flat. Slightly stained water limits visibility for sight-fishing somewhat, so supplement with a weedless gold spoon or soft plastic that fish can track by feel. With storms possible before 4 PM and Basin offering less weather protection than LaGrange, plan to be off the water or repositioned to a more sheltered spot by early afternoon.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer among the nearby bayous, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep interior holes provide year-round holding water for black drum and sheepshead. It's also the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the default choice when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is arguably the best all-around option today, combining the bay's best trout and redfish structure with the most weather protection available — a key advantage with storms possible before 4 PM. Hit the oyster bars at the mouth right around and after the 10:15 AM low tide, then work the incoming push as current activates the structure and pulls bait through. The recent guide report of a strong speckled trout bite bay-wide aligns perfectly with LaGrange's reputation, and slightly stained water will push trout tight to the bars where they're easier to target. Light WSW winds will barely affect this protected water, so you can fish comfortably through the morning and reassess when the afternoon storm window approaches.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where incoming tides push baitfish up the creek and concentrate redfish and trout in bends and along grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions to brackish water that holds bass alongside smaller redfish. Short and well-protected, it's considered the safest fishery in the area when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is a strong pick today specifically because it's the most weather-protected option near the marina — if the storm window before 4 PM has you wanting a quick exit, you're already close to the ramp. The incoming tide after the 10:15 AM low is the prime window; work bends and grass edges with soft plastics or live shrimp as bait gets pushed up the creek and reds and trout stack to intercept it. The creek mouth deserves attention for flounder on the tide change — a slow-dragged Gulp or paddletail along the bottom is hard to beat in slightly stained water. Light winds today won't be a factor inside the creek, so the main variable is simply timing your session to finish before storms build.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay, with summer mornings consistently producing trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular fishing pressure but produces reliably, and it sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous — run time is a real consideration.
hogtown.todaysCall: The recent Santa Rosa Beach guide report of a strong trout bite was likely tied to water like Hogtown — summer-morning grass flat action in 2–4 feet is this spot's signature, and today's conditions fit that script well. Plan to be on the flat at first light or shortly after the 6:04 AM sunrise to capitalize on the best morning bite before 85°F heat pulls fish off the shallows. The outgoing tide running toward the 10:15 AM low will concentrate fish on deeper grass edges; watch for Spanish mackerel at the mouth on the incoming push that follows. Factor in the longer run from the 331 Bridge when planning your storm exit — with a 29% storm chance before 4 PM, you'll want buffer time to get back safely.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport, and that direct connection means LaGrange's productive oyster-bar trout and redfish patterns plausibly extend into this quieter, less-pressured water. There's significantly less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself, so confidence here is lower than for its larger neighbor. Its small, interior character makes it a likely calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Think of Mallet Bayou as a bonus option if you're already fishing LaGrange — the same incoming tide that activates LaGrange's oyster bars after the 10:15 AM low could push fish up into Mallet's quieter water, particularly redfish nosing into the shallows. Light winds today mean the open bay is manageable, so Mallet's main appeal right now is reduced pressure rather than weather shelter — but that's still worth something on a summer weekday. Slightly stained water means feel-based presentations like weedless soft plastics or tipped jigs will outperform sight-fishing here. Given limited documentation on this spot, treat it as an exploratory add-on rather than a primary destination.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a genuine long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees less pressure simply due to its distance from the main ramps. It neighbors Hewett and Buck Bayou immediately to the east, making all three realistically fishable in a single trip.
mack.todaysCall: Mack Bayou's distance from the main ramps is both its appeal and its risk today — lighter pressure on fish is a real advantage, but the long run back with storms possible before 4 PM demands a disciplined turnaround time. If you commit to the run, be on the water at or just after the 6:04 AM sunrise and plan to head back no later than early afternoon. Work oyster bars and marsh grass edges on the incoming tide after the 10:15 AM low with soft plastics or weedless spoons suited to slightly stained water. Pairing this spot with Hewett and Buck Bayou on the same run makes the long trip more worthwhile — scout all three while conditions hold.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in a single trip. It offers the same protected-bayou habitat as its neighbors — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth with deeper interior holes further in — and sees light pressure due to its distance from the main ramps.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes best as part of a Mack-Hewett-Buck run on the 30-A side — the light pressure across all three bayous is the main draw, and today's manageable WSW winds make the run feasible. Time your arrival on the oyster bars and grass edges at the mouth to coincide with the incoming tide building after 10:15 AM, when redfish and trout will be most active on the structure. Slightly stained water calls for spoons, darker soft plastics, or lightly rattling jigs that help fish home in. With storms possible before 4 PM, the same caution applies here as at Mack — commit to an early-afternoon turnaround to make the run back comfortably.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there's less basis to speak with confidence about its fishing. It's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou makes the most sense as a third stop on a 30-A bayou run — if Mack and Hewett are producing, a quick exploratory cast through Buck's mouth and grass edges on the incoming tide is worth the minor detour. Don't plan your day around it given the limited fishing documentation, but the habitat should be consistent with its neighbors, and the same incoming tide push after 10:15 AM could position reds or trout near the mouth. Keep presentations simple in slightly stained water — a weedless gold spoon or soft plastic is easy to cast quickly while you assess whether the spot is holding fish. Storm timing is the same concern here as for the whole 30-A run; treat early afternoon as your hard stop.
